The collected writings of the philosopher Plotinus, who was born in Egypt, studied in Alexandria and taught in Rome from 244 until his death in 270. His student Porphyry edited the 54 treatises into six sets of nine; the Greek for nine gives the name.

The Enneads founded Neoplatonism, a new reading of Plato. Everything flows out from a single source, the One, through Mind and then Soul, down to the world of matter. The soul's task is to turn back and rise toward the One, which Plotinus said he had touched a few times.

These ideas ran deep into later religion. Augustine read Plotinus before his conversion. Greek Christian thinkers used him, and an Arabic version passed under the name "Theology of Aristotle" fed Muslim philosophers such as al-Farabi. Pagan Neoplatonists kept teaching in Athens until the schools were closed in 529.
